newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian euthanasia law survives latest challenge.
newsitem.headline: Australian euthanasia law survives latest challenge.

text.p: Australia's High Court on Friday adjourned a court challenge to the country's world-first voluntary euthanasia law, effectively guaranteeing the controversial law's continued operation well into next year.

Chief judge Frank Brennan said the court would not consider an application by a coalition of church, medical and aboriginal groups to challenge the legislation until the law's fate was considered by the national parliament.

A conservative government backbencher, with Prime Minister John Howard's support, has launched a private parliamentary motion for the government to use its constitutional powers to overturn the assisted suicide law which took effect in the outback Northern Territory in July.
But parliamentary officials said a final vote was not expected until at least March.
If there is no vote during the 10 sitting days in March, the parliamentary challenge could not be resolved until parliament resumes for the budget sitting in mid-May.
"It could take a long time (for parliament to resolve the issue," one official said.
Australia's constitution gives the national government the power to quash legislation passed by the two territories, but not laws passed in the six states.

The coalition mounting the High Court challenge, headed by Northern Territory doctor Chris Wake and aboriginal community leader and clergyman Djiniyini Gondarra, has already lost a move against the law in the territory's highest court.
Wake was not immediately available for comment.
The High Court case is the latest in a series of legal and political challenges to the territory's right to die legislation.
Although the law is widely condemned by Australia's political, religious and community leaders, opinion polls show about 75 percent of Australians support voluntary euthanasia.
The law, the world's first, began operating in July in the remote and sparsely-populated Northern Territory.
But legal and political wrangles have raised legal concerns for doctors and only one person has so far used the legislation.
That man, former carpenter and one-time Christian missionary Bob Dent, pleaded in a death-bed letter for parliament to allow the law to stand.

In a letter written on the eve of his September 22 suicide at his home in the territory capital, Darwin, Dent said the voluntary euthanasia law allowed him to "relieve this interminable suffering and to end my life in a dignified and compassionate manner".
"If you disagree with voluntary euthanasia, then don't use it, but don't deny me the right to use it if and when I want to go".
Dent's son, Rod, a member of Howard's Liberal Party, has also actively campaigned for the law since his father's death.
The doctor who helped Dent kill himself, Philip Nitschke, said several more people, fearing the law would be overturned by parliament, were applying for approval to use the law.
The territory legislation allows terminally ill Australians to commit suicide by lethal injection or pills if they meet tough guidelines.
